overview:
Canada is the second-largest country on Earth, stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and north to the Arctic Ocean. It covers about 9.98 million km², yet only about 40 million people live there, most of them within 200 kilometers of the border with the United States, the longest border between two countries in the world. Huge parts of the north are forest, tundra and ice.

The capital, Ottawa, sits on the river between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Canada has two official languages, English and French; most people in Quebec speak French, a legacy of the colony of New France. Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver are the largest cities, and immigrants from every continent have made them among the most diverse in the world.

Canada is a federation of ten provinces and three territories, a parliamentary democracy with a prime minister; the British monarch is head of state. First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples were here long before Europeans, and their cultures and rights are an important part of national life.
landAndNature:
Canada's landscapes are enormous: the jagged Rocky Mountains in the west, the flat wheat prairies, the ancient rock and lakes of the Canadian Shield, the rolling farms and forests of the east, and the treeless Arctic tundra where the sun barely rises in winter. The country has more lakes than any other, including four of the five Great Lakes shared with the United States. Niagara Falls roars on the Ontario border, and the Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world, rising and falling about 16 meters.

Winters are long and snowy across most of the country. Moose, beavers, grizzly and black bears, wolves, caribou and bald eagles live in the vast forests, while polar bears gather near Churchill on Hudson Bay each autumn and belugas swim in Arctic waters.
peopleAndCulture:
About one in five Canadians was born in another country, and cities buzz with dozens of languages beyond English and French. Hockey is the national winter sport and a shared passion; kids learn to skate on frozen ponds and backyard rinks. Lacrosse, a game invented by Indigenous peoples, is the national summer sport, and basketball was invented by a Canadian, James Naismith.

Maple syrup is the country's sweetest export; Quebec makes about three-quarters of the world's supply, and families visit sugar shacks in early spring. Poutine, fries with cheese curds and gravy, is a beloved comfort food, along with butter tarts and Nanaimo bars. Indigenous art, from totem poles on the Pacific coast to Inuit stone carvings, is celebrated nationwide. Canada Day on July 1 brings fireworks across the country.
history:
Indigenous peoples have lived in Canada for more than 12,000 years, from the Haida of the Pacific coast to the Inuit of the Arctic. Vikings briefly settled Newfoundland around the year 1000. French explorer Jacques Cartier arrived in 1534, and Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec in 1608, starting the fur-trading colony of New France. Britain conquered it in 1759–1763, and French speakers kept their language and laws.

On July 1, 1867, several colonies joined to form the Dominion of Canada, which grew westward with a railway completed in 1885. For over a century, the government forced Indigenous children into residential schools, a harm the country has formally apologized for. Canadians fought in both world wars, welcomed millions of immigrants, and gained full control of their constitution in 1982. Nunavut, an Inuit-governed territory, was created in 1999.
funFacts: Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined, by most counts more than two million.
Hawaiian pizza, topped with ham and pineapple, was invented in Ontario in 1962, not in Hawaii.
Letters addressed to Santa Claus, North Pole, postal code H0H 0H0, are answered by Canadian postal volunteers every year.
Insulin, the life-saving treatment for diabetes, was discovered in Toronto in 1921.
Mount Thor on Baffin Island has the greatest vertical cliff on Earth, a sheer drop of about 1,250 meters.
Canada's coastline is the longest of any country, more than 200,000 kilometers.
